justifications.functional_suitability: Claims Portal serves online submissions (R-01) and adjusters (R-02). Migration Router Component enables incremental claim-type migration (R-03) and fallback to legacy. Outbox Pattern Component, Sync Orchestrator, and Sync Ledger Table ensure reliable claim data exchange without data loss.
justifications.performance_efficiency: The sub-2s target (R-05) is addressed by serving adjusters from the modern State Store (Claim Operational Table) decoupled from the 5s mainframe via Integration & Sync Engine and Outbox Pattern Component. However, explicit read caching mechanisms are not defined.
justifications.compatibility: Mainframe coexistence is well supported via Legacy Mainframe Adapter Component, Mainframe Adapter (IBM MQ), and ExpressRoute. Active Directory federation is properly handled via OIDC/SAML and OAuth 2.0 within Authentication Client and Azure API Management.
justifications.usability: Claims Portal and Frontend UI provide web interfaces for both Customers & Brokers and Claims Adjusters. However, both user groups share a single generic portal without explicit differentiation in UI components for adjuster-specific workflows.
justifications.reliability: R-04 consistency is strongly addressed via Outbox Pattern Component, Integration & Sync Engine, Sync Ledger Table, and Resilience4j in Legacy Mainframe Adapter Component, preventing message loss or duplicate processing across systems.
justifications.security: R-07 is met with Active Directory SSO via Authentication Client and Azure API Management. Security Policy Enforcer, Security Policy Component (RBAC/ABAC), mTLS over ExpressRoute, Managed Identities, and Audit & Fallback Log provide thorough security.
justifications.maintainability: Migration Router Component and Temporal Tables support one-day rollback (R-06). Clear separation of concerns exists across components. However, choosing AKS for multiple services runs counter to the constraint that the team has little cloud experience.
justifications.portability: Target hybrid regions (on-prem and Azure West Europe) are well reflected via ExpressRoute, Azure App Service, and AKS. Technology choices like Spring Boot and Apache Camel facilitate container portability across environments.

PERF-01.justification: While Sync Orchestrator syncs data to Azure SQL, synchronous calls via Legacy Mainframe Adapter take up to 5s. Achieving sub-2s loads requires explicit asynchronous UI aggregation or pre-fetching mechanisms not fully articulated.
sensitivity_points: Synchronous mainframe SOAP latency directly impacts portal response times
Data freshness in Claim Operational Table versus live mainframe reads
tradeoffs: Serving stale pre-synchronized data improves response time but risks inconsistent state

PERF-02.justification: Submissions are accepted by AKS and persisted via Outbox Pattern to Azure Service Bus. Messages queue asynchronously, buffering spikes and preventing mainframe overload during batch windows.
sensitivity_points: Service Bus queue capacity and message retention during high-volume spikes
Throttling policy configuration on Azure SQL Resource Governor
tradeoffs: Asynchronous queuing increases ingest throughput at the expense of eventual mainframe consistency

AVAIL-01.justification: The Outbox Pattern Component and Azure Service Bus buffer incoming claims while the mainframe batch runs. Once the window closes, Apache Camel Sync Orchestrator drains queued submissions.
sensitivity_points: Service Bus queue depth handling 6 hours of queued batch data
Retry and backoff configurations in Resilience4j and Apache Camel
tradeoffs: Decoupling mainframe availability via queues delays downstream processing until morning

AVAIL-02.justification: Exactly-once guarantees are provided by Outbox Pattern, Sync Ledger Table watermarks, and Temporal Tables. Re-deliveries are deduplicated, ensuring no claim is lost or processed twice.
sensitivity_points: Idempotency keys and ledger watermark consistency across restarts
Dead-letter queue handling for unrecoverable sync payloads
tradeoffs: Strict ledger-based idempotency checks add latency to synchronization processing pipelines

MOD-01.justification: The Migration Router Component conditionally routes claims by type. Reverting or switching claim types is managed via configuration in the router and Audit & Fallback Log within hours.
sensitivity_points: Migration Router rule evaluation overhead on incoming requests
Synchronization ledger reconciliation speed during traffic cutover
tradeoffs: Dynamic routing rules increase component complexity to enable rapid switch-back capability

MOD-02.justification: Frontends communicate solely with APIM and Core services. Decommissioning the mainframe simply shifts Migration Router entirely to Claim Management, retiring legacy adapters without impacting UI layers.
sensitivity_points: Complete migration of legacy claims data into State Store
Decoupling of all legacy mainframe adapters from Core services
tradeoffs: Maintaining abstraction layers during migration adds overhead but isolates frontend from changes

SEC-01.justification: Security Policy Enforcer in APIM and Security Policy Component enforce ABAC/RBAC, denying cross-tenant broker requests. Unauthorized access attempts are recorded in the Audit & Fallback Log.
sensitivity_points: Attribute validation accuracy within claims tokens and policy components
Audit log immutability and alerting latency
tradeoffs: Fine-grained ABAC enforcement adds computational overhead to every API request

SEC-02.justification: Claims Portal federates directly with Active Directory, revoking platform access immediately upon AD account deactivation. However, synchronization of revocation to internal mainframe security tables (e.g. RACF) is not explicitly defined.
sensitivity_points: Token lifetime and session revocation propagation time across APIM
Deprovisioning latency between on-premises Active Directory and legacy mainframe
tradeoffs: Short token lifetimes improve revocation speed but increase authentication token renewal requests
